subtitle: כתאב אלאמאנאת ואלאעתקאדאת — The Book of Beliefs and Opinions
author: Saadia Gaon (882–942)
intro: The opening of Saadia Gaon's Book of Beliefs and Opinions (Kitāb al-Amānāt wa'l-Iʿtiqādāt) — the first systematic Jewish theology, written in Judeo-Arabic in 933 — in its original (FJMS manuscript). Saadia begins by praising God as the manifest Truth who grounds all certain knowledge, then states his purpose: to explain why doubt (shubha) befalls people in their inquiries and how it is dispelled, so that reason — which is built on the senses — can reach truth. Hover a phrase to see its English light up; tap any word for a gloss; dotted words are key terms.

terms.note: Saadia's title, usually rendered 'Beliefs and Opinions.' An amāna is a belief held with trust/credence; an iʿtiqād is a firm conviction one 'ties' onto (the root ʿaqada, 'to bind'). The book's aim is to move the reader from beliefs received on trust to convictions grounded in proof.

terms.gloss: the Truth, the Real — here a name of God
terms.note: Saadia opens by calling God al-ḥaqq al-mubīn, 'the manifest Truth/Real.' The same root yields ḥaqqan ('truly') and ḥaqāʾiq ('established truths'), and at the close of the passage al-ʿadl wa'l-ḥaqq, 'justice and truth' — the goal the seeker reaches.

The highest grade of knowledge in the philosophical tradition: not mere belief or probable opinion (ẓann) but assured, indubitable certainty. Saadia says God verified the rational soul's grasp of itself 'as a sure certainty,' ḥaqqan yaqīnan.

The key term of the Introduction. A shubha is not honest suspended judgment but a misleading resemblance or specious argument that 'befalls' a person (Saadia: sabab wuqūʿ al-shubha, 'the cause of doubt's befalling') and is mistaken for truth. The whole book sets out to dispel it.
Paired with shubha: once true knowledge is attained, 'the uncertainties departed' (zālat al-shukūk). Shakk is the ordinary state of wavering between two judgments, the opposite of yaqīn.

An indication that points the mind to a conclusion. Saadia promises to argue 'from the roots of the proofs (uṣūl al-dalāʾil), not their branches.' The seeker's failure, he says, is to make a real dalīl no proof, and a non-proof into one.
The strongest form of dalīl: an apodictic, conclusive demonstration. When knowledge is secure, Saadia says, 'the demonstrations cleared for them' (ṣafat lahum al-barāhīn).

Things grasped by the intellect (ʿaql) rather than the senses. Saadia's epistemic claim: the intelligibles 'have their foundations laid upon the sensibles' — reason is built up from sense-experience, so error in either can breed doubt.
Things apprehended through the five senses (al-ḥiss). For Saadia these are the first of the roots of knowledge and the foundation on which the intelligibles rest.

terms.gloss: inference — reasoning from evidence to a conclusion
terms.note: The act of drawing a conclusion from a dalīl. The first cause of error in reasoning, says Saadia, is that the seeker 'has no insight into the manner of inference' and so mishandles his proofs.

Disciplined theoretical reflection — the 'art' (ṣināʿa) one must complete before judging. The second cause of error is rushing 'to a verdict before completing the discipline of speculation.' Saadia treats naẓar as a religious duty.
